Both candidates follow the required four-section structure. Candidate A is concise and reasonable. It uses a few project details: the €4-6B contingency, the three phases, MAD costs, Tarifa/Tangier and the ICC arbitration. It is mostly generic, though, and includes some weak items. "Escalation triggers at 5%, 10%, 15% budget utilization" is an odd metric. "Blockchain tracking to prevent double-spending of materials" is gimmicky. Its audit procedures are fewer and less tied to project technical risks.

Candidate B is much more specific and decision-useful. It names distinct funds (maintenance trust fund, decommissioning reserve, marine mitigation fund, HVDC energy budget), quantifies potential losses, and ties risks to project features: rail operator collusion over gauge/ERTMS, seismic design cases, cetacean migration windows, hedging coverage, corrosion protection, and flooding drills. Its procedures cover technical, financial, workforce, and FX audits. Its transparency measures are broader and well tied to monitoring data and governance. It has some weaknesses. The invented figures (15-30%, €200-400M) are illustrative and unsupported. A few procedures drift from governance toward engineering or operations. The double-spending example is a little odd, and "permanent offshore residential platforms" may come from the upstream plan. It is also longer. Even so, it is far more useful for downstream stages and catches real risks that A misses, such as the maintenance fund and rail operator collusion. Overall B is better.

Candidate A is far more specific and plan-tailored. It cites reserves (contingency, maintenance trust fund, decommissioning, marine mitigation), cetacean seasonal restrictions, HVDC cable, ERTMS, currency hedging, and Tarifa/Tangier community agreements. Its risks are concrete, and its audit procedures state frequencies, thresholds, and scope. It also has more coverage in all four sections.

A has weaknesses. Some figures look invented or unverifiable, such as "inflating costs by 15-30%" and "claim 40% vs 25% progress". It also includes odd items, like offshore residential platforms used for tourism. It is verbose, and some procedures drift from governance audit into technical engineering audits. A few corruption items overlap. Even so, these details are decision-useful and consistent with the upstream documents it was given.

Candidate B is generic and short. It has only 6–7 items per section and thin procedures. Some content is questionable: "escalation triggers at 5%, 10%, and 15% budget utilization" is an odd metric, and blockchain tracking is a gimmick. It does reference the treaty, ICC arbitration, and multilateral development banks (MDBs), which are plausible plan-specific hooks. Its whistleblower and transparency measures are generic. Overall it is less useful downstream.

A is better on specificity, coverage, and usefulness.

A is more thorough, with 7, 8, 8, and 9 items across the four lists. It is concrete and tied to plan details (75% local sourcing, 60% tenant trigger, 70% FX hedge, 80% buffer, sovereign partition). Its audit procedures name frequencies, independent parties, and thresholds, and it covers procurement, EPC, land insider trading, and baseline manipulation. Its weaknesses are some invented cost figures, a conflation of the Phase 0 budget with remediation, and loose legal references. B is concise and anchored to the plan, with a few good insights such as the pre-FID RTE allocation audit and PPA misuse. But it has only 5 items per list, omits major corruption and procurement areas, and has the same Phase 0 budget conflation. A is more useful for downstream governance work.

Both follow the required four-section structure. A is concise (5 items per list) and ties to plan decisions (80% buffer = 128.8 km², 60% threshold, 70% FX hedge, sovereign partition segregation, PUE 1.20). Its items are plausible, though a few are weak: the PPA "unauthorized utilization" item, and "misallocation" items that are really strategic choices (e.g. PUE 1.15 vs 1.20). It also omits some vendor-kickback and insider-land-trading corruption risks. Its procedures are decent but fewer. One transparency measure, a public dashboard with 30-day lag, is realistic.

B is more comprehensive and detailed. It covers hardware vendor kickbacks, insider land speculation, information leakage, environmental baseline manipulation, double-billing of training costs, change-order abuse, PUE misreporting, and DGSI favor trading. Its procedures map one-to-one to the risks (independent re-certification, reconciliation, third-party PUE verification, tenant contract audit). Its transparency measures are broader (steering committee minutes, Sapin II, whistleblower, supplier code). Weaknesses: some invented figures (€200M–€500M, €100M–€300M, €30B–€40B hardware) that may not come from the plan. Sapin II is misapplied as a "transparency law" and it is not a public procurement transparency law. A "real-time" dashboard is shared with only internal stakeholders. The 20%+ contingency item is odd. There is also some confusion between the Phase 0 budget and remediation. Overall B is more specific, actionable and complete, and it better matches an audit framework for a mega-project. Its invented numbers are a modest flaw. Weaknesses in A's depth are larger.

Both follow the required four sections and cite upstream decisions (Decisions 2, 3, 10 and 12, the €900M grants, the €200M float, the 35 FTEs). I could not see the upstream documents, so I couldn't verify these references. B is more comprehensive and more specific. It covers standards capture, Technical Steering Committee conflicts of interest, float abuse as working capital, under-reporting of disruptions, gold-plating of the reference distributor, and shadow spending. It also gives eight procedures, each with an owner, a frequency and a trigger, and eight transparency measures such as a grant ledger, named votes and a backstop report. A is valid but thinner and more generic, and it omits audits of the reference distributor and of grant allocation. B's float range of "€200–€300M" is a minor ambiguity. Overall B is more useful for downstream governance planning.

Candidate A is more thorough and more useful for downstream planning. Each section has eight items. Each item is tied to a specific plan element: the €900M capacity-building grants, the €200–300M clearing float, the €150M reference distributor, the 35 FTEs, the 15 testing FTEs, Decisions 2, 3, 10 and 12, the T+5 and T+3 targets, and the month-6 and month-18 standards. The audit procedures name an auditor, a frequency and a trigger, such as the 150% float threshold, unannounced site visits and independent spot-checks. The transparency measures are concrete: public dashboards, a grant ledger, a named-vote record, a whistleblower portal, scoring rubrics and a backstop report. Each audit procedure maps onto a listed risk, and the transparency measures cover most risks.

A has minor weaknesses. The "Emergency Float Reserve €300M" is possibly slightly inconsistent with the €200M float. Some misallocation items are really misreporting or corruption, so the two lists overlap. It is also wordy.

Candidate B is correct and cites decisions and assumptions, for example Decision 9 on PRM reservation data and Decision 8 on reduction cards. It is much thinner, with five items per list. Several risks are generic, and some procedures lack an actor or cadence. It covers fewer areas. It has no grant ledger and no public auditing of enforcement. Its transparency measures are limited, with no public grant tracking or enforcement transparency. It does add a few useful points, such as the check for double funding from other EU sources and the PRM milestone audit. Overall it gives less decision-useful coverage.

Candidate A is much more comprehensive and decision-useful. Its corruption list has eight items covering contractors, transport kickbacks, staffing nepotism, kit conflicts of interest, registry misuse, and self-dealing. Its misallocation list is concrete: ghost shifts, double billing, falsified occupancy and contact rates to hit the Month 4 gate, kit degradation, and petty cash. Its audit procedures are tied to the Month 4 gate and the plan's metrics: a Month 3 audit before the gate, surprise cooling-center spot-checks, a 10% re-contact sample for outreach, installation verification, registry access-log audits, and dual sign-off on invoices. Its transparency measures are extensive. A has minor flaws: it invents specifics (10 centers, 5,000 kits, €1.2M staffing), mislabels the gate metric (80% utilization instead of 80% of planned hours delivered), treats thermometer installations as a gate trigger, and is long. Candidate B is better anchored in upstream decisions, the €300k reserve, and the thresholds, but it is thin, with five items per list. It misses key vectors such as registry misuse. It has no verification of installation counts and no re-contact sampling of outreach claims, which are the obvious gaming risks around the gate. It also proposes an "annual" reconciliation that fits poorly with a 12-month program. A is clearly more useful for downstream stages.

Both candidates follow the required four-section structure. Candidate A is concise and references specific strategic decisions and options (Decision 1, 6, 10, 12; Vulnerable Population Identification Modality; three-level thresholds). That suggests it used the upstream documents. Its content is plan-linked, but it is thin: five items per list. Some of its items are odd. One example is an "annual financial reconciliation" in a 12-month program. Another is a "Month 1 and Month 3" GDPR check of a "triage script". Its misallocation items are somewhat convoluted.

Candidate B is much more comprehensive and operational. It covers corruption risks that include GDPR data misuse and insurer leakage. Its misallocation risks are concrete: ghost shifts, double-billed transport, inflated occupancy and contact rates targeting the Month 4 gate, kit degradation, and fake installations. Its procedures are well-specified, with sampling rates, thresholds, timing tied to Month 3 and Month 4, dual sign-off, access-log audits, and installation verification. Its transparency measures are extensive and include a whistleblower channel, an equity audit, a community board, and published contracts.

B has some weaknesses. It invents specifics such as 5,000 kits, a €1.2M staffing line, and a 10-center network. These may or may not match upstream documents. Some figures are illustrative examples. It is also long, and some measures are excessive, such as the gender impact assessment and the 12-15 member board, which could be heavy for a pilot. Its "GPS-tagged receipt photos" could raise GDPR concerns. It does not cite the strategic decisions as explicitly.

Overall, B is more useful for a governance audit. It targets the gate-gaming risk that matters most and gives actionable audit procedures. A's tighter link to the plan's decisions is a plus, but its depth and procedural usefulness are much lower.
